title: Chapter 220 – Fifty-Four Winters
html:
[The Wall – Mo Yan]

Mo Yan is fifty-four years old, and she has not slept through a night in her life.

She sits at the window of her room in the Wall's east tower, wrapped in a gray shawl, with a candle burning low beside her and a white bell resting in her lap. Outside, the long black line of the Wall runs away into the dark. The beacon fires are low. The sentries pace. Far to the north, above the crack in the sky that has been her horizon for forty-five years, a few cold stars hang in the thin air, and she looks at them as a woman looks at a clock.

It is the hour before dawn. It has been the hour before dawn, in one way or another, for most of her life.

She is not a tall woman. She was never going to be. She is small and spare, with iron-gray hair cut short at the jaw and a face like a closed fist, and the hands in her lap are brown and knotted and scarred across the knuckles. She has a plain gray cloak. She has a plain gray tunic. She has, tucked into her sleeve where another woman might keep a handkerchief, a slim black ribbon with a hole in the middle. It is the ribbon she wore the day she came to the Wall. She has never replaced it. The hole is where her mother's name used to be.

Mo Yan, says a small clear voice in the bell.

"I'm here."

You're awake.

"I'm always awake."

I know. A pause. You shouldn't be. You're old now. You need sleep.

"I'm fifty-four, Sera. That's not old."

It is where I come from. A flicker of light along the crack. People died at forty. Mother used to say that a woman who reached fifty had won an argument with the world.

Mo Yan snorts. It is a short, dry sound. She has been having this conversation with the girl in the bell for forty-five years, in various forms, on various nights, and it has become a kind of liturgy. She says she is fine. Sera says she is not. They agree to disagree, and the candle burns down, and sometimes they sit in silence for hours, a woman and a bell, waiting for the end of the world.

Something's wrong, says Sera.

Mo Yan lifts her head.

---

It begins as a tremor in the floor.

She feels it through the soles of her feet before she hears it, a long slow shudder that runs up from the foundations of the tower and makes the candle flame lean. The window rattles. Somewhere below her a bowl falls from a shelf and rolls across the stone. She is on her feet with the bell in her hands before she knows she has moved.

It's the Seam, says Sera, very quickly. It's not attacking. It's—

"What?"

Eating.

The word hangs in the cold air.

Mo Yan goes to the window. The sky to the north has changed. The crack that has hung there for six hundred years, narrow and gray and patient, has begun to glow. It is a pale, sick, pearly light, like the inside of a shell, and it is spreading. She can see it pulse. She can see the long bright vein of it widen, a hair at a time, and a thin silver rain of sparks begin to fall from its lower edge toward the Wall.

It's drinking something, Sera whispers. A great deal. All at once. I can feel it going up.

"Up where?"

Up the Road. Up to the Door. The voice in the bell is small and urgent and very old. Mo Yan, there's a Terrace gone out. I felt it. A whole one. The hours, all at once.

Mo Yan's skin goes cold.

"Jian," she says.

I don't know.

"Yue. Hua. Veyra."

I don't know. I can't see them. I can only feel the light going. A hitch. I think the Orchard's burning.

For a moment Mo Yan stands very still.

Then she does what she has done every day for forty-five years when something terrible happens, which is to put the bell in the pocket of her cloak, and her hands on the window latch, and think only of the next thing.

The next thing is the tower.

---

They are all at the foot of the stair when she arrives.

The Wall has changed in forty-five years. It has grown, and slowed, and learned to live with its own long dread, as a house learns to live with the sound of the sea. There are three thousand people in the garrison now, and a hundred children, and a market in the lower court. There is a school. There is a kitchen larger than most inns, with long tables under a vaulted roof, where on festival days the whole Wall eats at once. And in the center of it, tall and slender and shining, there is the tower.

Han is standing at its door.

He is seventy-seven years old. He is a big man made small by time, with a back like a bent bow and a beard like frost on a gatepost, but he stands with his sword at his hip, and his white head high, and when he sees her coming he lifts a hand.

"You felt it," he says.

"I felt it."

"So did he." He nods up the spiral stair. "He's been awake since the first tremor. He won't see anyone. He says it's already begun."

"What has?"

"He didn't say." Han's seamed face is grim. "Qinghe's with him. And the Sect girl."

"Lan Xiu."

"She's not a girl, Mo Yan. She's sixty."

"She'll always be a girl to me."

Han almost smiles. It is a stiff, rusty movement, as of a gate that has not been opened. Then the tower shakes again, and the lantern swings, and he grips the doorframe. "Go up," he says. "I'll hold the base."

She goes up.

She has climbed these stairs ten thousand times. She could do it blindfolded. She counts, because counting is a habit, because the first time she climbed them she was nine years old and every step had been a mountain. Now every step is only a step, and she resents it a little, for being so easy. One hundred and nine. One hundred and forty. At the top, the door is open, and the round room beyond it is full of light.

---

It is blue light.

It pours from the great cracked window, thick as water, and it fills the high chamber from floor to ceiling. In the middle of it, in the high-backed chair where he has sat for forty-five years, Wenyuan is on fire.

Not with flame. With something quieter and more terrible. His white robe has gone translucent. His skin, under it, is the color of moonstone, a clear pearly white that glows from within, and she can see the faint dark lines of his veins as through a lantern of oiled paper. His hair is a halo. His blind brown eyes are wide open and fixed on nothing, and his mouth is moving, very slightly, in a litany she cannot hear.

Lan Xiu is kneeling at his feet.

She is a thin, upright woman in a pale blue robe, with a gray braid down her back and a face like an old drawing. She has her hands folded in her lap. In them is a small flat book, bound in dark leather. She is not reading. She does not need to. She has known its eleven lines for thirty years.

"It's the breakthrough," she says, without turning. Her voice is steady. "He's been at the edge for a decade. The Seam's surge has pushed him over."

"Nascent Soul."

"Yes."

"He's not ready."

"No." Lan Xiu's mouth tightens. "But the Seam doesn't care. It's pouring the Orchard's hours down the Wall like a river in flood. All he can do is drink or drown."

Mo Yan crosses the room.

She kneels beside Lan Xiu. The blue light is warm on her face, and the floor is trembling, and the white bell in her pocket is humming like a struck glass. She doesn't need Sera to tell her what is happening. She has seen it before, at the Wall, in the first year, when the Keystone sang.

"What do you need?" she says.

"The Cradle." Lan Xiu turns her head. In the blue glow her eyes are very clear. "He can't sing it. He's too far under. But you can. You paid. You're the one it listens to."

"I don't remember the words."

"I do."

"Then—"

"I'll say them. You sing them." A small, strained smile. "It's how we've always done it."

Mo Yan swallows.

She has sung the Cradle nine times in forty-five years. She sang it at the Wall's first Feast of the Roll, when the children asked. She sang it the night Elder Chao Wen died, in the Wall's infirmary, holding her hand. She sang it for the five pupils on the Quay of Bells, the summer Lan Xiu went back with the Sect's whole embassy and a hundred pairs of hands. She has never sung it for a man on the edge of Nascent Soul.

"All right," she says.

Lan Xiu opens the book.

---

It is not a long song.

Eleven lines, in a tongue Mo Yan has never studied and somehow always known. The first is a greeting. The second is a promise. The third is a name, or the place a name used to be, and every time she reaches it she feels the old hole in her chest tug, like a loose tooth. She sings it as Lan Xiu speaks it, line by line, in a low rough voice, a voice that is beginning to crack with age.

We remember you.

The light in the room steadies.

We have not gone.

Wenyuan's lips stop moving.

The door is open.

And something turns.

She feels it in her bones. A great slow wheel, shifting on its axle, a pressure that has been building for a decade finding its release. The blue light draws inward. It condenses. It gathers around the Keystone's slight figure like a cloak, and then, with a sound like a very long breath going out, it sinks into him, and is gone.

The room is dark.

For a moment, there is nothing. Only the candle, and the sound of three women breathing, and the thin high whine of the Seam beyond the glass. Then a voice says, mildly, from the chair:

"I wondered when you would stop."

---

He has changed.

She sees it as Lan Xiu lights the lamp. He is sitting exactly as he was, upright, his hands folded in his lap, his head turned toward the window. His face is the same: thin, calm, strangely young, with the smooth look of a man who has not seen the sun in forty-five years. But the skin has a grain to it now. A faint fine grain, like the surface of old marble, running along the cheekbones and the backs of his hands. When he turns his head, the light does not move on it. It sinks in.

"Master Wenyuan," Lan Xiu says. "Are you—"

"I am well." He lifts one hand and studies it, blindly, with a kind of mild interest. "I am a Nascent Soul cultivator. I have a seed. It is a very small one. It is the color of a plum." His mouth curves. "I cannot see it. I can feel it, very clearly, like a stone in my shoe."

"And the cost?"

"The cost is that I am the tower."

Mo Yan's chest tightens.

"I always was, to some degree." He turns his sightless face toward her voice. "But it was a thing of the feet, before. A sort of lending. A man may lend his feet to a building and take them back at night. Now—" He moves his fingers, slowly, one after another, in the lamplight. "Now it is the whole of me. The stone has come up through the knees, through the spine. It sits behind the eyes. I could not leave this room if I wished to. It would be like asking a candle to leave its flame."

"You can't walk," Lan Xiu says.

"I have not walked in forty-five years, child." His voice is gentle. "I have only learned to stop pretending."

Nobody speaks.

Mo Yan reaches out and takes his hand. It is cool, and smooth, and slightly gritty, like a river pebble. It does not return her grip. She holds it anyway.

"What did the tree ask you?" she says.

"What tree?"

"It's an expression."

"Ah." He smiles. "The Seam asked me what I was for. I told it I was the thing that holds." A long breath. "It said that was a good answer. And then it said, for how long?"

"What did you say?"

"I said, until someone comes to take my place." He tilts his head. "I think that was a mistake."

---

Mei arrives at first light, in a closed cart, with a stick across her knees.

Mo Yan sees it from the east gate, where she has gone to take the air and drink a bowl of tea, and for a moment she does not believe it. The cart is a plain brown thing, drawn by a patient gray mare, and it is followed by four riders in the Hall's gray tunics. It has traveled hard. The wheels are caked with the red mud of the northern road. The driver climbs down stiffly and goes to the back to lower a step.

The woman who descends is sixty-four years old.

She is small, and straight, and entirely white. Her hair is pinned in a tight braid down her back, silver-white from the brow, with no trace of the dark that once ran under it. She leans on an ash stick. She wears a gray cloak over a plain gray robe, and she has the lined, quiet, careful face of a person who has spent a lifetime reading small print by lamplight. When she lifts her head and her eyes meet Mo Yan's across the courtyard, they are exactly the same eyes.

"Hello, Mo Yan," says Mei.

Mo Yan finds that she cannot move.

It is absurd. She is a woman of fifty-four. She has stood on the Wall in the worst winter of the century and held a bell against the Seam. But there is something in the voice, the dry kindness, the faint amusement, that goes through her like a blade, and for one long second she is a child of nine again, in a stolen cloak, in a tower, with the cold in her bones and a hole where her mother's name used to be.

"You came," she says.

"I felt it too." Mei crosses the courtyard, one careful step at a time. "The tremor. It went through the Hall at the third bell. The Roll woke, all two thousand of them, in one breath. I thought it was the end." A dry smile. "Hai Ren said that if it was, we might as well go to the Wall. She said at least we'd have company."

"Hai Ren's well?"

"Hai Ren is seventy-one and bossy as ever. She sends her love. And a very rude message for Han."

Mo Yan laughs. It cracks in her throat.

Mei reaches her. They stand face to face in the pale light of the courtyard, the old woman and the older child, and for a moment neither of them speaks. Then Mei lifts a thin hand and lays it against Mo Yan's cheek. It is cool and dry and a little shaky.

"You grew up," she says.

"I had to."

"I know." Her eyes are bright. "I'm sorry I wasn't there for it."

"You sent me letters."

"I sent you forty-one letters in forty-five years. That's not the same."

"It was enough."

"It was not." Mei's mouth trembles. "It was never enough. But it was what I had."

Mo Yan takes the hand from her cheek and holds it in both of hers. For a time they stand like that, in the courtyard, and the cart-horse shifts and blows, and the riders look elsewhere with the careful tact of people who have been told not to stare.

"Is she with you?" Mo Yan says at last.

"Little Mei?" Mei's face softens. "She's in the cart. She wouldn't stay behind. She's fifty-two years old, and I've not been able to tell her what to do since she was eleven."

The cart door opens.

A woman steps down: tall, spare, brisk, with a round dark face and a head of cropped gray curls. She wears the apron of a healer and carries a satchel on her shoulder. She stops at the foot of the step and looks around the courtyard, at the beacon fires, the high black wall, the tall shining tower, with an expression of mild professional curiosity. Then she sees Mo Yan, and her whole face changes.

"Oh," she says.

She does not run. She is fifty-two. But she walks across the courtyard very quickly, with her satchel banging at her hip, and when she reaches Mo Yan she stops dead and holds out both arms like a child.

Mo Yan steps into them.

The embrace is brief and fierce and a little awkward, the clumsy hug of two women who have been writing to each other for half a century and have never had the practice. Little Mei smells of lamp oil and dried herbs. Her heartbeat is steady against Mo Yan's cheek, a strong, slow, even beat, with no skip in it.

"You're alive," Mo Yan says, stupidly.

"So are you."

"I'm a lot older than I expected."

"Everyone is." Little Mei draws back, and her dark eyes are shining. "Show me the tower. Aunt Mei says there's a man in it who needs a physician."

"He needs more than that."

"Then I'll bring tea."

They go in together, the three of them, across the courtyard and through the tower door, Mei leaning on her stick and Little Mei carrying her satchel and Mo Yan walking between them with her hand in her pocket on the white bell. At the foot of the stair Han is waiting. He takes in the white-haired woman and the brisk healer with a single glance, and something in his big ruined face gives way.

"Mei," he says.

"Han." She inclines her head. "You've shrunk."

"You've gone white."

"It suits me."

"It does." He clears his throat. "Hai Ren's message. Did she send one?"

"She said you were an old goat."

"That's the polite version."

"I know," says Mei, serenely. "I cleaned it up."

Han laughs. It is a deep rusty bark, and the sentries at the door turn their heads in astonishment. Mo Yan has not heard him laugh like that in twenty years. She thinks, with a small tight ache under the ribs, that this is what the Wall has been waiting for: not a victory, not a sign, not an end to the war. Just three old friends meeting on a stair, and a joke told badly, and the light coming slowly into the east.

---

Qinghe goes at midday.

They find her in the kitchen, which is where she has been since the first tremor. She is standing at the long iron stove with a wooden spoon in her hand, stirring a pot of porridge, and the porridge is bubbling merrily, and the whole vast room smells of milk and cinnamon. She is a short broad woman of seventy-two, with a face like a good loaf of bread and a hairnet over her white curls. She looks, as she has looked every day of Mo Yan's life, entirely and unshakably ordinary.

Her shadow is gone.

Mo Yan sees it first. She stops in the kitchen doorway with her hand on the frame. The noon sun is pouring through the high windows, and the long tables, the benches, the stacked bowls, the hanging pans, each of them throws a shadow across the stone floor. The cook does not. She stands in a pool of light with the sun full on her back, and the floor at her feet is bright and bare.

"Qinghe," she says.

"Hmm?" The woman does not turn. She is tilting her head to the left, listening to the pot. "Mind the door, dear, it sticks."

"Your shadow."

"Oh, that." A comfortable sigh. "Yes. I noticed it about an hour ago. I was standing in the larder and I thought, what a very odd thing, I've gone and lost myself." She taps the spoon on the edge of the pot. "I had a funny turn, you see. In the night. I was sitting in my chair by the fire and I felt it go. Like an egg cracking."

"Nascent Soul."

"I'd not know what to call it." Qinghe's eyes, in her round brown face, are cloudy and kind. "I only know I woke up feeling a great deal younger. And rather hungry." She finally turns around. "And I've no shadow. Isn't that queer?"

Mo Yan opens her mouth.

She cannot think of a single thing to say.

"Don't fuss," says Qinghe, comfortably. "It's only a cost. They always are. I'd rather lose a shadow than a tongue." She pauses. "Or a husband. Or a child. Or the use of my hands." She smiles. "It could have been a good deal worse."

"It could have been your cooking."

"Heaven forbid." The cook laughs, a rich warm bubbling sound. "I've always said, if I lose my cooking, you may put me in the ground. Now sit down, the pair of you, and eat. You look like two ghosts."

They sit.

They eat porridge in the noon light, in the vast warm room, while the Wall wakes around them and the Seam, beyond the northern ramparts, falls slowly silent. Mo Yan finds that she is ravenous. She eats two bowls without noticing, and a third because Qinghe puts it in front of her and watches her with those cloudy kind eyes until she does. She finds that her hands are shaking. She finds that Lan Xiu, across the table, has put down her spoon and is staring into her bowl with a fixed, bright, unseeing gaze.

"Lan?"

"I'm all right."

"You're not."

"I'm thinking about the Terrace." The old pupil lifts her head. "I was thirty when I went back, Mo Yan. I took a hundred of the Sect's best, and the Cartographer's book, and I sang the Cradle for three weeks. We woke the five. We woke seventeen of the Keepers. We woke—" She swallows. "We woke the girl with the braid. Pei. She laughed. She said I'd got fat."

"I remember."

"But the others wouldn't wake. There were four hundred, and only seventeen would. The rest—" She shakes her head. "I think they were waiting for something. I never knew what."

"A voice that isn't afraid."

"A voice that has paid." Lan Xiu looks at her. "I think there's another price. One we haven't found."

Mo Yan is silent.

In her pocket, the white bell has gone quiet. It has been quiet for an hour. She puts her hand on it, through the cloth, and feels the thin cool line of the crack, and waits.

Mo Yan, says Sera, at last.

"I'm here."

He's coming.

She stops with her spoon halfway to her mouth.

"Who?"

The one who burns. The voice is very small. I felt him when the hours went up. He was standing at the top of the Road. He turned around. And he looked down.

Mo Yan sets down her spoon.

He's looking for the one who sings, says Sera.
